text: The first documented speculative excess ended in February 1637 without any bad news to trigger it, because no more buyers could be found.
lang:
The tulip came to the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century. The coveted flamed patterns were caused by a mosaic virus and could only be passed on through daughter bulbs, so supply was biologically limited. The bulbs could be stored and traded. In winter they existed only on paper for the purposes of trade, and so forward trading arose in goods that nobody saw. At the same time, the Netherlands was the richest trading nation in Europe and had a functioning capital market.

At the auction for the Alkmaar orphanage on 5 February 1637, tulip bulbs fetched around 90,000 guilders. Two days earlier, on 3 February 1637, not a single bulb had found a buyer at a tavern auction in Haarlem. The collapse was preceded by neither new information nor a crop failure nor a tax. Trading broke off because nobody was bidding any more.

Prices fell by more than 95%. The outstanding forward contracts were largely not honoured. In Haarlem, buyers were able to cancel them in 1638 for a fee of 3.5% of the purchase price. The Dutch economy continued to develop unimpaired after 1637.

For comparison, an average annual income was about 150 guilders, or around 300 for skilled workers according to other sources. For the Semper Augustus variety, prices of 1,000 guilders (1623), 5,500 (1633) and 30,000 for three bulbs (1637) are recorded, though partly from contemporary pamphlets. In her research, Anne Goldgar documents only around 285 people involved in Haarlem, about 60 in Amsterdam and about 25 in Enkhuizen. The image of a mass mania comes mainly from Charles Mackay's book of 1841.
lehre: A market collapses when the next buyer fails to appear. No bad news is needed for that.

titel: Mississippi Bubble and John Law's paper money
text: The same institution issued the shares and at the same time printed the money to buy them. In this way it drove the price upwards in a circular process.
lang:
After the death of Louis XIV, France was heavily in debt. The Scotsman John Law founded the Banque Générale in 1716, which was nationalised in 1718 as the Banque Royale, and in 1717 the Mississippi Company, with trading monopolies in Louisiana. Investors exchanged government debt securities for shares in the company, and the same institution printed the banknotes with which the shares were paid for.

The share price rose from 500 livres in 1717 to around 10,000 livres in December 1719, and forward contracts were briefly quoted at up to 14,000. It then fell to around 1,000 livres in December 1720 and back to 500 in September 1721, around 95% below the peak price.

Money creation drove prices up. In January 1720 French inflation reached around 23% a month (not a year). In November 1720 the paper money was abolished, and France returned to a metallic currency. Distrust of paper money and joint-stock banks shaped French financial policy for decades.

The word “millionaire” comes from this episode. Investors who sold early and switched into tangible assets kept their wealth. The other holders of the securities saw both the share and the money lose value.
lehre: When the same body issues the security and prints the money used to buy it, the price says nothing about the value of the security.

text: South Sea Company shares rose to just over seven times their initial price within seven months, and by December they were almost back at their starting level.
lang:
The South Sea Company, founded in 1711, held a trading monopoly for South America that yielded practically no income. Its business model was essentially based on an exchange. When it was founded, it had already taken over around £9 million of British government debt and issued its own shares in return. In January 1720 it offered to take over around a further £31 million in the same way, and in April 1720 Parliament agreed. The higher the share price, the fewer shares it had to hand over for the same debt. The company therefore had a direct interest in a rising share price and promoted it with loans to buyers and gifts to members of Parliament.

The share price rose from around £128 in January 1720 to around £950 in July. After 18 August it fell from over £800 to £200 and reached its low of £124 in December. Compared with the July high, that was a fall of around 87%.

In June 1720 Parliament passed the Bubble Act, which prohibited the formation of joint-stock companies without royal authorisation. The act hampered British corporate finance for more than a hundred years. Isaac Newton lost around £20,000 on the venture.

Newton had initially sold at a profit and then bought back in at peak prices. The quotation attributed to him about the predictability of the heavenly bodies and the unpredictability of people is not documented in contemporary sources. It is regarded as a later attribution and has come down to us only as an anecdote.
lehre: Intelligence does not protect against mistakes in a bubble. Newton sold at a profit and bought back in at peak prices.

titel: Panic of 1873 in Vienna and Berlin
text: Five billion francs in French reparations first set off a wave of company formations, which was followed by a wave of bankruptcies.
lang:
After the Franco-Prussian War, France paid reparations of 5 billion francs in gold from 1871 onwards. An estimated 2.5 to 3 billion of this flowed directly into the capital markets. At the same time, the 1870 amendment to stock corporation law made it considerably easier to found new companies. In Prussia, around 928 joint-stock companies and 61 new banks were established between 1871 and 1873. In the years 1867 to 1870 there had been 88 companies.

On 9 May 1873 the Vienna Stock Exchange collapsed. Within hours more than 120 banks became insolvent, and the exchange closed at 13:00. The crisis reached New York on 19 September 1873 and from there spread back to Europe.

Between December 1872 and December 1874, the shares of 444 German companies lost around 2 billion marks in market value. Many of the newly founded companies had no business model apart from an issue prospectus.

The widespread interpretation that the Panic of 1873 (Gründerkrach) ushered in a continuous “Long Depression” lasting until 1896 is disputed among researchers, because growth rates in those years were not negative throughout. The pattern described is considered established, but the overall interpretation is not.
lehre: A sudden inflow of money from outside reliably leads to a wave of company formations, followed by a wave of bankruptcies.

text: In 1914 one US dollar cost four marks twenty, and in November 1923 around 4.2 trillion marks.
lang:
From 1914 the German Reich financed the war through bonds and the printing press instead of taxes, and suspended the convertibility of the mark into gold. After 1918, reparations were added. When French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr in 1923, the Reich government likewise paid for the passive resistance with newly printed money.

The exchange rate rose from 4.20 marks per US dollar on 1 July 1914 to 49,000 in January 1923, 760,000 in July, 53 million in September and 4.2 trillion marks per dollar on 20 November 1923. That corresponds to an increase by a factor of one trillion. Such a series can only be shown on a logarithmic axis.

Monetary assets, bonds, passbook savings and life insurance policies became practically worthless. Owners of tangible assets and debtors emerged from the inflation stronger, because loans could be repaid with devalued money. The inflation therefore did not hit everyone equally. It shifted wealth from creditors to debtors.

On 15 November 1923 the Rentenmark was introduced, and from 20 November 1 Rentenmark equalled 1 trillion paper marks. Inflation ended practically at once, although the new currency was only formally backed by land charges (Grundschulden) on the landed property of agriculture, industry and commerce and could not be converted into gold. In economics, this is therefore referred to as the “miracle of the Rentenmark”. The highest denomination ever issued was 100 trillion marks. The first note of this value went into circulation in November 1923.
lehre: Currency depreciation proceeds exponentially and, viewed linearly, is underestimated until the very end.

titel: Wall Street Crash of 1929 and the Great Depression
text: With a loss of 86% in the index and around 25 years until the old level was regained, this was the deepest decline in the history of the US stock market.
lang:
The 1920s brought a long bull market that was increasingly financed with credit. Brokers financed more than two thirds of the purchase value. Outstanding loans for securities purchases exceeded $8.5 billion, and thus the entire stock of US cash in circulation at the time. The Dow Jones reached its peak of 381.17 points on 3 September 1929.

On Black Thursday, 24 October 1929, 12.9 million shares were traded. On Black Monday, 28 October, the index fell by 12.82%, and on Black Tuesday, 29 October, by 11.73% on a volume of 16.4 million shares. Over the two days together it lost 23.05%. Most of the damage, however, only occurred afterwards.

The predecessor of the S&P index lost a total of 86.2% over 32.8 months, from its high on 7 September 1929 to its low on 1 June 1932. The Dow fell to 41.22 points by 8 July 1932, around 89% below its high, and did not close above that high again until 23 November 1954. The 25 years apply to the price index excluding dividends. Adjusted for inflation and with dividends reinvested, the recovery came earlier.

The crisis was intensified by developments outside the stock market. Around a third of all US banks disappeared between 1930 and 1933, the Federal Reserve allowed the money supply to shrink by about 30%, and the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 triggered retaliatory tariffs worldwide and a decline in trade. Unemployment rose to around 25% in the USA, and in Germany from an annual average of around 1.9 million in 1929 to more than 6 million in February 1932. Industrial production fell by 46.8% in the USA and by 41.8% in Germany.
lehre: The statement “the market always recovers” is true, but it says nothing about how long an investor has to hold out until the recovery.

text: In the middle of the recovery, monetary and fiscal policy applied the brakes at the same time, and the index again lost more than half its value.
lang:
After the low of 1932, the US stock market had recovered strongly, and the economy was growing again. Out of concern about inflation and for the sake of budgetary discipline, policymakers tightened policy. The Federal Reserve raised the banks' minimum reserve requirements, and the government consolidated the budget.

The S&P index fell by 54.5% within 12.8 months, from its high on 6 March 1937 to its low on 31 March 1938. The setback thus came in the middle of a recovery that was still incomplete, and not at the end of a period of euphoria.

The old high was not regained until 5 February 1946, almost nine years after the high of March 1937.

The year 1937 is regarded as the standard example showing that exiting a crisis policy is itself a risk. The same trade-off arises at the end of every period of low interest rates.
lehre: Exiting a crisis policy is itself a risk, because if tightening comes too early, the downturn starts all over again.

text: With the new currency, the shop windows filled up immediately, and savers bore the cost of the preceding inflation.
lang:
Since 1936 the Reichsmark had been kept artificially stable by a price freeze and rationing, while war financing had created an enormous monetary overhang. This gave rise to a barter economy in which goods were held back and cigarettes served as a substitute currency. Between February and April 1948, under the code name Operation Bird Dog, the Allies secretly brought around DM 5.7 billion in cash, weighing about 500 tonnes, into the country.

On 20 and 21 June 1948 the Deutsche Mark was introduced. Everyone immediately received a per-capita allowance of DM 40 and a further DM 20 within two months. Wages, rents and pensions were converted at 1:1, savings balances initially at 10:1. In effect, savers received DM 6.50 for every 100 Reichsmarks.

The reform worked immediately. The black market disappeared, and the shelves filled up because hoarding goods was no longer worthwhile. The goods had therefore been available; what had been missing was a currency in which it was worth selling them.

The burdens of the reform were unevenly distributed. Monetary assets lost around 93.5% of their nominal value, while tangible assets, property and production facilities were preserved in real terms. A homeowner in 1948 still owned the house afterwards, while a saver kept about one fifteenth of the balance.
lehre: A currency depends on trust, and price controls cannot replace that trust. The cost of inflation is borne by the holders of monetary assets.

text: After a long bull market, high valuations and a political conflict were enough for a decline of 28%.
lang:
The post-war bull market had raised valuations considerably. In the early 1960s, rising real interest rates came on top of this, along with an open conflict between President Kennedy and the US steel industry over price increases, which made the political risks for companies visible.

The S&P 500 fell by 28.0% from its high on 12 December 1961 to its low on 26 June 1962. There was no recession during this period.

The old high was regained on 3 September 1963, 630 calendar days or around 20.7 months after the high. This was followed by a strong upward phase until the credit crunch of 1966.

The Kennedy Slide is the earliest well-documented example showing that a decline of more than a quarter does not require an economic crisis. A high entry price is enough.
lehre: A decline of more than a quarter does not require a recession. High valuations are enough.

text: An inverted yield curve and a tight central bank were enough for this bear market. There was no recession.
lang:
The financing of the Vietnam War and an overheating economy forced the Federal Reserve into a restrictive policy in 1966. The yield curve inverted, that is, short-term interest rates rose above long-term rates. Credit became scarce and expensive even before the real economy weakened.

The S&P 500 fell by 22.2% from its high on 9 February 1966 to its low on 7 October 1966. Formally this was a bear market, although no recession followed.

The old high was regained on 4 May 1967, 449 calendar days or around 14.8 months after the high.

The episode shows that credit conditions are a factor in their own right. Share prices depend on profits, and also on the interest rate at which these profits are discounted and on how easily companies can refinance themselves.
lehre: When short-term interest rates rise above long-term rates, credit becomes more expensive long before the recession becomes visible.

text: The market lost 36% and took more than three years to return to its old level, without a single dramatic crash day.
lang:
In the late 1960s inflation and interest rates rose, the yield curve inverted again, and a recession followed in 1969/70. Unlike 1929 or 1987, there was no single day with a spectacular collapse. Prices gave way over a period of a year and a half.

The S&P 500 fell by 36.1% from its high on 29 November 1968 to its low on 26 May 1970.

It took 1,193 calendar days, or around 39.2 months, until the old high was regained on 6 March 1972. Of this period, eighteen months were accounted for by the decline and a further twenty-one by the recovery.

The subsequent recovery passed directly into the Nifty Fifty euphoria and thus into the next, considerably deeper bear market of 1973/74. Two bear markets in quick succession occur again and again.
lehre: There are often more months between the low and the old high than between the high and the low.

titel: Nixon shock and the end of Bretton Woods
text: Since 15 August 1971, no money in the world has been convertible into gold.
lang:
The Bretton Woods system tied the currencies of the industrialised countries to the US dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35 per fine ounce. US budget deficits and the financing of the Vietnam War increased the quantity of dollars in circulation, while US gold reserves did not grow with it. More and more central banks demanded gold instead of dollars.

On 15 August 1971 the USA unilaterally ended the convertibility of the dollar into gold. With the Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971, the dollar was devalued to $38 per fine ounce. In March 1973 Bretton Woods finally came to an end, and floating exchange rates took its place.

Since then, all money has been pure fiat money, whose value rests solely on the credibility of the issuing central bank. Gold rose to around $850 per fine ounce by 1980, and the 1970s saw double-digit inflation rates.

The consequences are measurable to this day. The German consumer price index stood at 125.8 points in August 2026, against a base of 2020 = 100. A basket of goods that cost €100 in 2020 costs around €126. Cash has thus lost around a fifth of its purchasing power in six years, without there having been a crash.
lehre: Since 1971, loss of purchasing power has been the norm and not an exception. An account that pays no interest loses purchasing power continuously.

text: Around fifty blue chips were regarded as shares you never have to sell, and on average they traded at around 42 times their earnings.
lang:
After the volatile 1960s, institutional investors in the USA concentrated on a group of fast-growing blue chips such as Coca-Cola, McDonald's, IBM, Xerox, Polaroid, Avon and Disney. There was never an official list of the Nifty Fifty. The term describes an investment attitude and not an index.

Around 1972, the average price-to-earnings ratio of these shares stood at roughly 42, while the long-term market average was about 15 to 20. The reasoning was that the quality of these companies justified practically any price, because you would never sell the shares anyway.

In the bear market of 1973/74, the Nifty Fifty performed considerably worse than the market as a whole. This was not due to the companies, as many of them still exist today and are profitable. The cause was the entry price, which already anticipated every assumption about future growth.

More than a fifth of these shares had a price-to-earnings ratio above 50, while the market average was 15 to 20.
lehre: An excellent company is not automatically an excellent investment. The purchase price makes the difference.

titel: Oil crisis and the stagflation bear market of 1973/74
text: A supply shock hit highly valued shares, and it took seven and a half years to return to the old level.
lang:
Bretton Woods had collapsed, inflation was already rising, and valuations were high after the Nifty Fifty phase. The conditions for a deep decline therefore already existed before the triggering news arrived.

After the OAPEC embargo in October 1973, the oil price rose from around $3 to over $5 per barrel, and in the following year to just under $12. In West Germany there were four car-free Sundays from 25 November 1973 and a temporary speed limit of 100 km/h on motorways, which applied from November 1973 to March 1974. In 1974 West Germany spent just under DM 23 billion on crude oil, around DM 14 billion more than in the previous year.

The S&P 500 fell by 48.2% from its high on 11 January 1973 to its low on 3 October 1974. The old high was not regained until 17 July 1980, after 2,744 calendar days, or around 90 months or seven and a half years. Because of the double-digit inflation of those years, the real loss was considerably greater still than the nominal loss.

Stagflation, that is, rising prices combined with falling output, is the worst case for a mixed portfolio, because equities and bonds fall at the same time and cash also loses value in real terms. The second oil crisis of 1979/80 drove the oil price to a peak of around $38 per barrel.
lehre: Monetary policy does little against a supply shock, and equities, bonds and cash lose value at the same time.

titel: Silver speculation by the Hunt brothers
text: The Hunt brothers failed in their attempt to dominate the silver market when the exchange changed its rules.
lang:
In the late 1970s, investors afraid of inflation increasingly put their money into precious metals. The Texan Hunt brothers bought silver on a large scale, physically and through futures contracts, and financed the purchases mainly with credit. They assumed that they could determine the price if they held a sufficiently large part of the available supply.

At the end of 1979, Hunt companies controlled around 195 million fine ounces. The price rose from under $10 in mid-1979 to $34.45 on 31 December 1979 and to over $50 in January 1980. The value of the position grew from around $1.1 billion at the end of July 1979 to around $6.8 billion at the beginning of January 1980.

In January 1980 the exchange changed the rules. On 7 January COMEX introduced position limits, and from 21 January it only permitted closing-out transactions, so that new purchases were practically impossible. On 27 March 1980, Silver Thursday, the price fell to $10.80, around 78% below the January high. The Hunts could no longer meet their margin calls.

A consortium of 13 banks provided $1.1 billion in credit to prevent a chain of payment defaults on the futures markets. In 1988 came a civil judgment of around $134 million and bankruptcy under Chapter 11, and in 1989 a settlement with the regulator, the CFTC.
lehre: Leverage that you cannot service in an emergency is first and foremost a payment obligation.

text: Key interest rates of around 20% ended high inflation and at the same time triggered a severe recession.
lang:
After two oil crises, US inflation was in double digits and the central bank's credibility was damaged. In 1979 Paul Volcker switched the Federal Reserve to targeting the money supply and deliberately accepted that interest rates would rise to wherever the market set them.

Key interest rates reached around 20%. The S&P 500 fell by 27.1% from its high on 28 November 1980 to its low on 12 August 1982, accompanied by a severe recession and high unemployment in industry.

The old high was regained as early as 3 November 1982, 705 calendar days or around 23.2 months after the high and just under three months after the low. Prices turned when the news was at its worst.

August 1982 marked the start of the bull market that lasted until 2000. At the same time, a forty-year phase of falling interest rates began, which supported the bond markets and only ended in 2022.
lehre: Bear markets end when the news is at its worst. This point can never be recognised at the time.

text: The largest one-day loss in the history of the Dow Jones occurred without a recession, solely as a result of automatic hedging sales.
lang:
It was preceded by a strong bull market accompanied by rising interest rates. What was new was portfolio insurance, a computer-based hedging strategy that automatically sells futures when prices fall. It works as long as only a few market participants use it. If they all apply it at the same time, each sale triggers the next.

On 19 October 1987 the Dow Jones lost 508 points or 22.6% in a single day. That was the largest one-day loss in its history. The DAX, calculated retrospectively for this period, fell by 9.39% to 1,321.61 points on the same day. Over the course of the month, the stock markets in Hong Kong lost 45.8%, in Australia 41.8%, in the UK 26.4% and in Canada 22.5%.

The total drawdown of the S&P 500 was 33.5%, measured from the high on 25 August to the low on 4 December 1987. The pre-crisis high was regained on 26 July 1989, 701 calendar days after the high. Despite the record loss, the S&P 500 ended 1987 with a gain.

As a consequence, the NYSE introduced circuit breakers in 1988. These are trading halts at specified price losses, intended to break the feedback loop between falling prices and automatic sales.
lehre: When all market participants use the same automatic hedge at the same time, it amplifies price falls instead of protecting against them.

text: The Nikkei 225 took 34 years and two months to regain its 1989 high.
lang:
After the Plaza Accord of 1985, the Bank of Japan cut interest rates significantly. Banks granted loans with land as collateral. Rising land prices allowed new loans, with which shares and more land were bought. In this way the stock market and the property market drove each other upwards.

The Nikkei 225 closed at 38,915.87 points on 29 December 1989, and its intraday level was 38,957.44. At the peak, land in Tokyo's Ginza district cost ¥30 million per square metre. The 1.15-square-kilometre grounds of the Imperial Palace were considered more valuable than all the property in California. This contemporary estimate had no official basis, but it vividly illustrates the price level of the time.

Between May 1989 and August 1990, the Bank of Japan raised its key interest rate from 2.5% to 6.0%: to 3.25% on 31 May 1989, 3.75% on 11 October 1989, 4.25% on 25 December 1989, 5.25% on 20 March 1990 and 6.00% on 30 August 1990. This tightening is regarded as the trigger for the bursting of the bubble. By the low of 7,054.98 points in March 2009, the index had fallen by around 81.9%. Some sources give 80% or 81% and other lows. Prices for prime locations in Tokyo fell to less than 1% of their peak by 2004.

The Nikkei did not reach a new all-time high until 22 February 2024, at 39,098.68 points, after 34 years and two months. That is the longest known recovery time of a major benchmark index. The index then continued to rise rapidly, to 40,000 points on 4 March 2024, 50,000 on 27 October 2025, 55,000 on 9 February 2026 and 72,366.34 points on 25 June 2026.
lehre: Investing in a single home market is not diversification, and 34 years without a new high is a real scenario.

titel: Gulf War and US recession of 1990
text: An oil price shock, a recession and the savings and loan crisis cost the market a fifth of its value, and after seven months the loss had been recovered.
lang:
The US economy weakened in 1990, weighed down by the savings and loan crisis. Hundreds of savings institutions had got into difficulties through interest rate risk and risky property loans and had to be wound up with taxpayers' money.

On 2 August 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait, and the oil price jumped. The S&P 500 fell by 19.9% from its high on 16 July 1990 to its low on 11 October 1990, remaining just below the threshold for a bear market.

The old high was regained as early as 13 February 1991, 212 calendar days or around seven months after the high. The recovery set in when the course of the war became foreseeable, and thus well before the recession officially ended.

The episode contradicts the widespread notion that deep declines mean long recoveries. Depth and duration are largely independent of each other.
lehre: The depth of a decline says little about its duration. A loss of a fifth can be recovered within seven months.

text: Fixed exchange rates concealed the risk of foreign currency debt until Thailand abandoned its dollar peg.
lang:
The South-East Asian economies were growing strongly and attracting capital. Their currencies were pegged to the dollar, which made foreign loans appear safe. Banks borrowed money in foreign currency and lent it out in local currency. Such a currency mismatch only works as long as the exchange rate holds.

On 2 July 1997 Thailand abandoned the baht's peg to the dollar, and the currency immediately depreciated by 15% to 20%. As a result, debts in dollars, measured in local currency, became more expensive overnight, while income continued to arise in local currency. Capital flight spread to Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and South Korea. The Hang Seng fell by around 60% from its high on 7 August 1997 (16,820 points intraday) to its low on 13 August 1998.

In 1998 Indonesia's gross domestic product shrank by 13.1%, Thailand's by 7.6% and South Korea's by 4.9%. South Korea's unemployment rate rose from 2% (1996) to 6.8% (1998). The International Monetary Fund paid out around $39 billion, subject to strict conditions. Bilateral and multilateral lenders had pledged around $85 billion in total.

For the S&P 500, the crisis amounted to no more than a correction of minus 10.8% from 7 to 27 October 1997, which had already been recovered by 5 December 1997. The same crisis can therefore hardly matter for a globally diversified portfolio and yet be devastating for a single market.
lehre: Debts in a foreign currency carry exchange rate risk. A fixed rate conceals this risk but does not eliminate it.

text: A fund with two Nobel laureates as partners and leverage of more than 25:1 fell so deeply into losses within four months that fourteen banks had to rescue it.
lang:
Long-Term Capital Management was founded in 1994 and counted the Nobel laureates Robert Merton and Myron Scholes among its partners. The fund pursued convergence trades. It bet on small price differences between similar bonds that had reliably converged in the past. Because the profit margins were very small, the model needed high leverage. Returns after fees were around 20% in the partial year 1994, around 43% in 1995, around 41% in 1996 and around 17% in 1997.

At the beginning of 1998, equity of $4.7 billion was matched by around $124 billion of debt, which corresponded to leverage of more than 25:1. In addition, there were derivatives with a notional volume of around $1.25 trillion. After the Russian default on 17 August 1998, all positions moved against the fund at the same time, because all market participants were switching into safe investments simultaneously. The fund lost $4.6 billion in less than four months. On 25 September 1998, equity stood at $400 million and leverage at more than 250:1.

On 23 September 1998 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York organised a rescue of $3.625 billion by 14 institutions. No taxpayers' money was involved, but the unwinding was coordinated in order to avoid fire sales. The S&P 500 lost 19.3% during this phase (high on 17 July, low on 31 August 1998) and had recovered the loss by 23 November 1998.

The subsequent interest rate cuts intensified the final phase of the dotcom bubble. The rescue of a single fund thus changed the course of monetary policy as a whole, and with it the conditions for the next bubble.
lehre: Models describe normal market phases. Whether an investor survives exceptional phases depends on their leverage.

text: The Nasdaq Composite lost 78%, even though the underlying technology prevailed.
lang:
The internet provided a credible new growth story, and the interest rate cuts after 1998 provided cheap money. Companies went public without profits and were valued by the number of clicks. The price-to-earnings ratio of the Nasdaq was about 200 at the end of 1999, more than double the figure of 80 at the peak of the Japanese bubble.

The Nasdaq Composite reached its high of 5,048.62 points on 10 March 2000 and fell to around 1,114 points by 9 October 2002, a decline of 78%. By the end of 2002, around $5 trillion in market value had been wiped out. Accounting scandals such as Enron and WorldCom, as well as 11 September 2001, prolonged the descent.

The broad market fell less far but took longer. The S&P 500 lost 49.1% from 24 March 2000 to 9 October 2002 and did not regain its old high until 30 May 2007, after 2,623 calendar days or around 86 months. After the period from 1973 to 1980, this is the second-longest phase without a new high since the Second World War, and it passed directly into the financial crisis. For the DAX, sources give two peak values for 7 March 2000, 8,064.97 and 8,136.16 points. Measured against the low of 2,202.96 points on 12 March 2003, this gives a decline of around 73%, the largest since the index began in 1988. A new DAX high only came on 13 July 2007, at 8,151.57 points.

In 2004, 48% of the dotcom companies still existed, though at far lower valuations. Cisco lost around 80% of its market value, and Pets.com closed nine months after its IPO. Amazon and eBay became the big winners, even though the market as a whole lost 78%.
lehre: A technology can prevail and the price can still have been too high. It is the purchase price and not the idea that determines the return.

text: The selection index of the Neuer Markt lost more than 96% in 31 months, and around €200 billion in market value was wiped out.
lang:
The Neuer Markt was launched on 10 March 1997 as a stock exchange segment for young growth companies. Its admission and disclosure rules were considerably looser than those of the official market. The Nemax All Share and the selection index Nemax 50, which was introduced on 1 July 1999, have a base of 1,000 points as of 30 December 1997.

The Nemax 50 reached its all-time high of 9,666 points on 10 March 2000 and fell to 318 points by 9 October 2002. That was a loss of more than 96% in 31 months.

More than 300 companies were listed, and around €200 billion in market value was wiped out. The segment was closed on 5 June 2003. For many German private investors, the Neuer Markt was their first experience of shares and, for years, their last.

The accounting scandals showed the consequences of the loose rules. For years ComROAD reported almost exclusively fictitious revenue, and there were also the cases of EM.TV and Infomatec. A segment with low requirements inevitably attracts companies that could not meet higher requirements.
lehre: A stock exchange segment with loose rules attracts companies that would not meet stricter rules.

text: Risk that had been bundled, rated and sold on still existed, but could no longer be recognised.
lang:
After 2001 interest rates were low, and US house prices rose until 2006. Subprime mortgages, that is, loans to borrowers with weak creditworthiness, accounted for around a fifth of newly originated US residential mortgage loans between 2004 and 2006. These loans were securitised and bundled, and rating agencies rated the bundles AAA. Banks, insurers and local authorities all over the world bought these securities.

On 9 August 2007 trading on the interbank market largely came to a standstill, because no bank knew any longer what risks the others had on their books. On 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. The S&P 500 fell by 56.8% from its high on 9 October 2007 to its low on 9 March 2009. The DAX fell from 8,151.57 points (13 July 2007) to 3,666.41 points (6 March 2009), that is, by around 55%, and ended 2008 down 40.37%. At the same time, on 13 October 2008 it recorded its largest one-day gain since its launch in 1988, at plus 11.40%.

The S&P 500 did not regain its old high until 28 March 2013, after 1,997 calendar days or around 65.6 months. The International Monetary Fund estimated worldwide asset losses up to April 2009 at around $4.1 trillion. Industrial production in the euro area fell by more than 20% within a year, and the government debt ratio of today's 27 EU member states jumped from 65.1% of GDP (2008) to 75.7% (2009). In this way the banking crisis turned into a sovereign debt crisis.

Central banks responded with zero interest rates and quantitative easing. This policy shaped the following decade and made possible the longest bull market in US history, lasting until 2020. The fact that the DAX's largest one-day gain since 1988 fell in the middle of the crisis is no coincidence, because the best and the worst days lie close together.
lehre: Risk that is bundled, rated and sold on still exists. It becomes harder to recognise and therefore greater.

text: Within minutes the Dow Jones lost just under 1,000 points and immediately recovered most of it.
lang:
By 2010 US equity trading was largely automated. Liquidity, that is, the ability to buy or sell at any time, came mainly from algorithms that can withdraw their quotes within milliseconds when markets become turbulent, and on 6 May 2010 they did so.

On that day the Dow Jones fell at times by more than 9%, or just under 1,000 points. The S&P 500, already down more than 4%, fell by a further 5% to 6% within about four minutes and partly recovered in the following 20 minutes. Between 14:40 and 15:00 New York time, around 2 billion shares were traded. Individual shares briefly fell by up to 99% because there were no longer any bids.

The joint report by the SEC and the CFTC traced the trigger to an algorithmic sale of E-mini futures contracts worth $4.1 billion. The selling program set its pace solely according to current trading volume and sold faster the more was traded. Later the London day trader Navinder Singh Sarao was prosecuted. For years he had placed large sell orders and immediately cancelled them again, earning around $40 million in the process.

As a consequence, from June 2010 trading in a share in the S&P index was suspended for five minutes if it lost more than 10% within five minutes. Since 2013 the Limit Up-Limit Down rule has applied instead. It does not permit any trades outside a price band around the average price of the preceding five minutes, and it halts trading for five minutes if the price does not return to the band within 15 seconds. For private investors, the most important point is that a sell order without a price limit can be executed at any price whatsoever during such minutes.
lehre: A market's liquidity only applies to the moment at hand. It disappears in periods of stress, when investors need it most urgently.

text: A single sentence from Mario Draghi calmed the markets before any money had been spent on it.
lang:
After 2008, bank risks became sovereign risks. In October 2009 Greece revised its budget deficit from 3.7% to 12.7% of gross domestic product. The debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 104.6% (2007) to 128.5% (2009). For the first time, investors asked themselves whether the government bonds of a euro member could default.

There followed rescue packages of €110 billion (May 2010), €164.4 billion (2012 to 2014) and €86 billion (2015 to 2018, of which €61.9 billion was paid out). In March 2012 came the largest debt restructuring in history. Private creditors waived 53.5% of the face value, which corresponded to a loss of around 75% in present value terms. The DAX fell from 7,527.64 points (2 May 2011) to 5,072.33 points (12 September 2011), a decline of 32.6%. It ended 2011 down 14.69%. The S&P 500 lost 19.4% between 29 April and 3 October 2011. It was additionally weighed down by the dispute over the US debt ceiling and the downgrade of the USA from AAA to AA+.

On 26 July 2012 ECB President Mario Draghi said at the Global Investment Conference in London: “Within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.” Spreads fell without the announced programme ever being used. In monetary policy, expectations are an instrument in their own right.

For Greece, the economic consequences were nevertheless severe. Gross domestic product shrank by around 26% between 2008 and 2013, and unemployment reached around 26% in 2014. Capital controls applied from June 2015. On 5 July 2015, 61.3% of voters rejected the conditions in the referendum, and in August 2018 the last programme ended.
lehre: Government bonds are not risk-free. Even within a monetary union, creditors can lose part of their money.

titel: China shock and oil price slump of 2015/16
text: A devaluation of the yuan and an oil price below $30 were enough for a decline that dragged on for nine months.
lang:
China's growth was slowing, and the domestic stock market had fallen sharply in 2015 after a credit-financed rally. In August 2015 the Chinese central bank unexpectedly devalued the yuan. Investors took this as an admission of economic weakness.

At the same time, the oil price fell below $30 per barrel. This hit the US energy sector, which had financed its shale oil production heavily through bonds, and raised fears of a credit crisis in the high-yield segment.

The S&P 500 fell by 14.2% from its high on 21 May 2015 to its low on 11 February 2016. The old high was regained on 11 July 2016, 417 calendar days or around 13.7 months after the high.

The episode is instructive because it never became dramatic. There was no crash day and no collapse of a major institution, and formally it was not even a bear market. Nevertheless, a slow decline over nine months feels longer to investors than a deep, rapid slump.
lehre: A decline of less than 20% can drag on for a year and demand more staying power than a deeper, faster crash.

titel: Volmageddon and the interest rate shock of 2018
text: There were two setbacks in one year, first from the collapse of volatility products and then from the Fed's tightening.
lang:
After years of unusually calm markets, products that bet on persistently low fluctuations had become established. Their buyers earned money as long as fluctuations remained low. At the beginning of February 2018 volatility jumped, and the best-known of these securities, above all the XIV certificate, lost practically all of their value. The S&P 500 fell by 10.2% from 26 January to 8 February 2018 and had recovered the loss by 24 August 2018.

The second phase had a different cause. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates and at the same time reduced its balance sheet, and on top of this came the trade conflict between the USA and China. The S&P 500 fell by 19.8% from its high on 20 September to its low on 24 December 2018, remaining just below the bear market threshold of 20%.

The recovery began when the central bank changed course. After this so-called Powell pivot, the old high was regained on 23 April 2019, 215 calendar days after the high. The DAX had already reached its all-time high of 13,596.89 points on 23 January 2018 and gave up around a fifth by December.

Two separate lessons can be drawn from 2018. First, a product that bets on calm markets is worthless in turbulent markets. Second, monetary policy moves prices in both directions, and often faster than the economy does.
lehre: A product that bets on permanently calm markets becomes worthless as soon as markets turn turbulent.

text: With a loss of 33.9% in 33 calendar days, this was the fastest bear market in history.
lang:
Until mid-February 2020 the US indices were at all-time highs. Then it became apparent that the pandemic could not be contained within China, and within weeks the markets priced in a worldwide standstill.

The S&P 500 fell by 33.9% from its high on 19 February to its low on 23 March 2020. Never before had a market fallen so quickly from an all-time high into a bear market. The Dow lost 2,997.10 points or 12.93% on 16 March, 2,352.60 points (minus 9.99%) on 12 March and 2,013.76 points (minus 7.79%) on 9 March. The volatility index VIX closed at a record 82.69 on 16 March. On an intraday basis, the DAX fell by just over 40% from its high on 17 February to its low on 16 March, and on a closing price basis by just under 39% from 19 February to 18 March. On 12 March it lost 12.24%, the second-largest one-day loss in its history.

Policymakers responded faster than ever before. On 15 and 16 March the Federal Reserve cut its key interest rate to a range of 0% to 0.25% and launched bond purchases of $700 billion. According to the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), the six US relief acts of 2020 and 2021 together provided around $4.6 trillion, more than $2 trillion of which came from the CARES Act of March 2020 alone. The S&P 500 had recovered its loss by 18 August 2020, 181 calendar days after the high. The DAX ended 2020 up 3.55% at 13,718.78 points.

Investors who sold in March 2020 in order to wait for the situation to become clearer missed the recovery of the following months. By the time the news finally became clear, prices were already higher than before the pandemic.
lehre: The low point and the best time to buy lie close together, and both can only be recognised in hindsight.

titel: Meme stocks and the GameStop short squeeze
text: One share rose by around 2,700% in four weeks and then lost more than 80% within two days.
lang:
The rise was fuelled by zero interest rates, direct government payments to households, commission-free trading apps and forums such as WallStreetBets, in which investors coordinated with one another. At the retail chain GameStop, around 140% of the freely tradable shares had been sold short on 22 January 2021, that is, more shares than were freely available at all. Short sellers have to buy the shares back later, and if the price rises, the pressure to do so grows.

The share started January at $17.25 and reached an intraday high of $483 on 28 January 2021, and more than $500 in pre-market trading. That was a rise of around 2,700% since the start of the month. On the same day, several brokers restricted buying because the clearing houses raised their collateral requirements. The DTCC raised the industry-wide requirements from $26 billion to $33.5 billion. On 29 January Robinhood raised an additional $1 billion in capital.

On 1 and 2 February the share lost more than 80% compared with its intraday high, 60% on 2 February alone, to a closing price below $100. Around $27 billion in market value was lost. The hedge fund Melvin Capital, which had bet on falling prices, lost 53% of its value by the end of January and received $2.75 billion in fresh capital, $2 billion of it from Citadel and $750 million from Point72.

Short interest fell to 39% by 1 February and to around 25% of the free float by 8 March. This removed the mechanism that had forced the rise, and the price fell. Private investors can learn two things from this. A price that arises without any connection to the business has no floor when it falls. In addition, the tradability of a position depends on third parties who can change their rules at short notice.
lehre: A price that rises without any connection to the business has no floor when it falls.

titel: Inflation surge and turn in the interest rate cycle in 2022
text: Equities and bonds fell at the same time, and the classic mixed portfolio offered no protection.
lang:
After years close to zero, inflation rose sharply from 2021 onwards. For Germany, annual averages of plus 3.1% (2021), plus 6.9% (2022) and plus 5.9% (2023) are reported, and the highest monthly figure was around 8.8% in October and November 2022.

The S&P 500 fell from its high on 3 January 2022 to its low of 3,577.03 points on 12 October 2022, a decline of 25.4%. The triggers were inflation above 8%, the Federal Reserve's fastest cycle of rate rises since the 1980s, the war in Ukraine and the energy price shock. The DAX lost around 27% and ended the year down 12.35%. It recorded its largest one-day gain of the year on 9 March 2022, at plus 7.92%.

What was unusual was less the depth of the decline than its simultaneity. Because interest rates rose from an extremely low level, bond prices fell in parallel with share prices. A portfolio of 60% equities and 40% bonds, for decades the standard allocation for reducing risk, lost on both sides. In July 2022 the ECB ended eight years of negative interest rates by raising the deposit facility rate from minus 0.50% to 0.00%. By September 2023 it had raised it to 4.00%.

The old high was regained on 19 January 2024, 746 calendar days or around 24.5 months after the high. That is considerably longer than after the much deeper coronavirus crash, which had been recovered after 5.9 months. The German consumer price index stood at 125.8 points in August 2026 (2020 = 100). A basket of goods that cost €100 in 2020 therefore costs around €126.
lehre: The depth of a decline says little about its duration. A shallower slump can last considerably longer than a deeper one.

text: Banks came to grief over government bonds that were safe from default, because they had to sell them early.
lang:
The interest rate rises of 2022 and 2023 lowered the prices of long-dated bonds. A bond with a 1% coupon can only be sold at a discount when new securities offer 4%. Silicon Valley Bank had invested customer deposits in such securities. At the end of 2022 it had more than $15 billion of unrealised losses on its books. In addition, about nine tenths of its deposits of around $175 billion were above the deposit protection limit, so that customers had every incentive to withdraw their money immediately if they had doubts.

On 9 March 2023 customers withdrew $42 billion in a single day. On 10 March the bank, with total assets of $209 billion, collapsed. That was the third-largest bank failure in US history. It was followed on 12 March by Signature Bank, with around $88.6 billion in deposits, and on 1 May by First Republic, which was sold to JPMorgan for $10.6 billion. From 12 March the Bank Term Funding Program supported the banks. Across the US banking system as a whole, there were more than $600 billion of unrealised losses on the books.

On 19 March 2023 UBS took over Credit Suisse, founded in 1856, for CHF 3 billion in shares. Subordinated AT1 bonds worth CHF 16 billion were written down in full, while the shareholders still received something. This reversed the usual order of ranking in insolvency. The Swiss National Bank provided up to two times CHF 100 billion in liquidity. This had been preceded by customer outflows of CHF 110.5 billion in the fourth quarter of 2022 and by the losses from Archegos (around CHF 5 billion) and Greensill. In the first quarter of 2023 customers withdrew a further CHF 61.2 billion, and in the second quarter, after the takeover, another roughly CHF 39 billion. The share price fell from over CHF 90 (2007) to CHF 1.55 on 15 March 2023.

The broad market, by contrast, barely reacted. The S&P 500's maximum intra-year drawdown in 2023 was 10.3% and occurred in the period from 31 July to 27 October, that is, months after the bank failures. The year ended with a gain of around 26% including dividends. Problems at individual institutions do not necessarily spread to the market as a whole.
lehre: Interest rate risk is a real risk. Even a bond that is safe from default can lead to ruinous losses if it has to be sold early.

titel: Unwinding of the yen carry trade in 2024
text: A comparatively small interest rate rise in Japan cost the Nikkei 12.4% in one day.
lang:
For decades Japan kept its interest rates at zero or below. This gave rise to the carry trade. Investors borrowed in yen, invested the money in currencies with higher interest rates and kept the interest rate differential as income. This works as long as the yen does not appreciate, because the debt is denominated in yen but the assets are not.

When the Bank of Japan raised interest rates in 2024, the yen appreciated and the positions had to be closed. Because many market participants had entered into the same trade, they sold at the same time. On 5 August 2024 the Nikkei 225 lost 12.4% in one day. Between 16 July and 5 August 2024, the S&P 500 recorded its maximum intra-year drawdown of 8.5%. Measured against the turmoil in the markets, that was a moderate figure.

The S&P 500 ended the year up 24.9% including dividends. In the same year, on 22 February, the Nikkei 225 surpassed its old all-time high for the first time since 1989, and it reached 40,000 points on 4 March.

In 2024 Bitcoin also became an investment for institutional investors. In January the US regulator approved spot ETFs, and in April the fourth halving followed, in which the block reward fell from 6.25 to 3.125 BTC. The price reached $73,664 in March and, for the first time, $100,000 in December. In each of the four preceding cycles there had been drawdowns of between around 77% and 93%. Such declines are part of the usual pattern for this asset.
lehre: A trade that rests solely on an interest rate differential ends abruptly on the day the differential shrinks.

text: Just over four months passed from the all-time high through a slump and back to a record.
lang:
The year began in January with the DeepSeek shock. The assumption that leading AI models necessarily required enormous computing capacity was called into question, and Nvidia lost 17% in one day. This suddenly put up for debate the valuation of the company that had contributed most to the market's rise in the previous years.

The bigger slump followed the tariff announcements of 2 April 2025. The S&P 500 fell by 18.9% from its high on 19 February to its low on 8 April. In the process, more than $5 trillion in market value was lost over two trading days, more than ever before in two days. On 9 April, one day after the low, the index rose by 9.5% in a single day after a 90-day tariff pause had been announced.

The index reached a new all-time high as early as 27 June 2025, at 6,173 points, 128 calendar days after the old high. The DAX fell by around 21% from around 23,476 points in March to 18,489 points on 7 April. On 20 May it was quoted above 24,000 points for the first time, and it ended the year at around 24,490 points, a gain of about 23%.

This makes 2025 the most compact example of one of the few robust rules in market history, according to which the best and the worst days lie close together. An investor who remained continuously invested in the S&P 500 from 1996 to 2025 turned $10,000 into $192,167. Without the ten best days, they would have had 56% less, and without the thirty best, around 84% less. Of the 50 best days, around 76% fell in a bear market or in the first two months of a new bull market.
lehre: Investors who get out after a slump are not invested on the day of the rebound, and the rebound often follows only a few hours later.

titel: Energy shock and turn in the interest rate cycle in 2026
text: In 2026 imported supply-side inflation forced the ECB in June and the Fed in September to reverse course.
lang:
After the easing cycle of 2024/25, the ECB's deposit facility rate stood at 2.00% in June 2025, the low point of the cycle. The energy price shock resulting from the conflict in the Middle East brought about a turnaround in the course of 2026.

The figures show a pure supply shock. In June 2026 energy price inflation in the euro area was 8.5% (10.8% in May), headline inflation 2.8% and the core rate excluding energy and food only 2.4%. In the USA, headline inflation of 3.4% in August 2026 compared with a core rate of 2.4%. The core rate was therefore a full percentage point below the headline rate. Going by the headline rate alone, you would considerably overestimate domestic price pressure.

In September 2026 both major central banks tightened their monetary policy. The ECB had already raised the deposit facility rate to 2.25% in June and increased it to 2.50% with effect from 16 September, and the main refinancing rate to 2.65%. On 16 September the Federal Reserve decided to raise its target range to 3.75% to 4.00% with effect from 17 September. In Germany the inflation rate was 2.9% in August 2026 and 2.8% in July.

On the stock markets, the year remained calm up to that point. The S&P 500's maximum intra-year drawdown was 9.1% between 27 January and 30 March 2026, so formally it was not even a correction. On 13 August 2026 the index closed at an all-time high of 7,798.99 points (intraday 7,816.70). It had first closed above 7,000 points on 15 April 2026. On 17 September it closed at 7,637.76 points, around 2% below the high. The DAX reached an intraday all-time high of 26,618.74 points on 28 August 2026, after having stood above 26,000 points for the first time on 3 August. The ECB projections of September 2026 expect inflation of 3.0% for 2026, 2.5% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028. On this basis, the inflation target would only be reached again in 2028.
lehre: A supply shock shows up in the headline rate and not in the core rate. The central bank can only fight it through expectations, because it cannot influence supply.
